modules.title: Property & Land: Building Wealth You Can Pass Down
modules.summary: For most Zambians, the path to generational wealth runs through land. Learn to buy safely, avoid the traps, and build a portfolio you can pass on.

lessons.title: Why land is one of the few inflation-beating assets most Zambians can buy
lessons.content:
# Why land is one of the few inflation-beating assets most Zambians can buy

Zambians have few assets that beat inflation. Land is one of them — and the one most easily bought badly. It is also not a savings account: need K50,000 in three months and land will not give it to you.

## What you are actually buying

You never own land outright in Zambia. All land is held from the State on a **renewable 99-year lease** granted by the Lands Commission, and allocation does not confer ownership. Buying land means buying the **leasehold**, and the State must consent to the transfer. Your proof is the **title deed** issued in your name by the **Lands and Deeds Registry**.

## The case for land

Asking prices in 2026 ran from **K20,000–K45,000** for a small 20m × 20m plot in Chongwe to **K550,000–K700,000** for a titled 1-acre parcel in Silverest, Lusaka. These are **asking** prices, not assessed values.

**Services move the value**: plots that gain power and water after you buy are reported to appreciate **40–60% within 6–12 months** in the satellite areas; plots that never get them do not. A titled leasehold plot can be built on, rented, sold, mortgaged or inherited.

The risks are real too. Land is **illiquid** — you cannot sell a plot you do not yet own. It carries **legal risk** if the seller is not the registered owner. It costs **ground rent every year**, and an unserved plot **earns nothing** while you wait.

## The fees you must budget

| Item | Amount | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Property Transfer Tax (PTT) | **5%** of the contract sum or the ZRA-assessed value, whichever is higher | On the **transfer**, not on land you already own. ZRA says the **seller** pays; some cost tables say the buyer. It is negotiable — **ask who is paying: it changes the price you agreed** |
| Consent fee (transfer to Zambians) | **K333.60** | Lands and Deeds Registry fee chart |
| Title registration | **Sources conflict — confirm before you transfer money** | One source: **1% of value, capped at K15,000**. Another: **2% of market value**. The cap matters more on expensive land. **Get the current figure in writing from the Lands and Deeds Registry or your lawyer** |
| Ground rent | **K3,833.40 per year** for residential medium-cost land in Lusaka, Kitwe, Ndola and Livingstone | Set by regulation. Ask for the ground rent receipt — the Commissioner of Lands refuses consent if it is unpaid |
| Municipal property tax ("rates") | **No published schedule was found** | Ground rent is a State charge, not the same thing. Ask your local council |
| Standard build cost | roughly **K8,000–13,500 per square metre** | K242 per square metre is an outlier, not the market rate. Land and connections add another **15–30%** on top |

**PACRA does not register land.** PACRA registers companies and intellectual property; land is registered at the **Lands and Deeds Registry** under the Lands and Deeds Registry Act (Cap 185).

## The land-buying checklist

1. **Search the title at the Lands and Deeds Registry** for the title number and the registered owner's name, and get a **certificate of result of search**.
2. **Confirm the seller is the registered owner**, or holds a **registered power of attorney**.
3. **Inspect the plot physically** with two witnesses, and take dated photographs.
4. **Never pay the full price before the title is searched.** Pay in small instalments against receipts, and never pay the balance before the deed is in your name.
5. **Watch for a double sale** — the same plot sold twice, often to two buyers who both believe they own it.
6. **Walk away from "K100 today, the rest when the title is ready."** That is the commonest shape of land fraud in Zambia.
7. **Check the agreement names the plot number, the title number and the date.**
8. **Confirm who is paying PTT**, and get the **ground rent receipt** before you pay.

## If you cannot afford to build

There is no Zambian "National Housing Corporation". The body is the **National Housing Authority (NHA)**, set up under the National Housing Authority Act (Cap 195, 1971). It lends for acquiring land and constructing approved houses on it, over periods of up to **30 years** for individual housing loans, and runs a **10,000-unit** programme at Lusaka South MFEZ for purchase or rent-to-own. The **current individual loan rate is not published**, so ask the NHA for it **in writing** before you budget.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Write down three plots you want, with the plot number and asking price for each.
> 2. Ask the Lands and Deeds Registry what a title search on one of them would cost, and what the current registration fee is.
> 3. Optional: ask your local council for the property tax (rates) schedule for your plot.

> **Where to check**
> The Lands and Deeds Registry, Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, Lusaka — for title searches, the current registration fee and ground rent.

modules.title: Teaching Your Family About Money: Generational Wealth
modules.summary: The most important financial skill you can teach your children is not saving — it is thinking. Build a family financial habit that survives you.

lessons.title: The "money talk" most Zambian families never have
lessons.content:
# The "money talk" most Zambian families never have

Most Zambian families never talk about money. It is called rude, private, or dangerous to ask. That silence — not a lack of knowledge — is why financial habits do not pass from one generation to the next.

## The numbers that explain the silence

| Indicator | Zambia |
|---|---|
| Financial inclusion | **80.1%** (up from 69.4% in 2020) |
| Financial health | **39.1%** (up from 13.6% in 2020); the benchmark is 51% |
| Use mobile money | 76.2% of adults |
| Use a commercial bank | 30.1% of adults |
| Saved using mobile money | 65.8% of adults |
| Saved at a bank | 15.4% of adults |
| Emergency money from family, relatives or friends | 34.9% of adults |
| Emergency money from savings | 11.1% of adults |

Read the gap: **80.1% of Zambians are inside the financial system, but only 39.1% are financially well.** More than one adult in three says family is where emergency money comes from; only about one in nine says savings. (Bank of Zambia FinScope 2025; World Bank Global Findex 2025.)

## Hold one money talk a quarter

Thirty minutes, same room, one set of numbers everyone can see. Not a lecture.

1. **What do we earn?** Every income that enters the household, including side income and the "small money" never written down.
2. **What do we owe?** Every loan, every mobile money debt, every family loan not written down, and the school fees coming.
3. **What do we save?** How much leaves the household on payday, where it sits, and what it is for.
4. **What are the rules?** A fixed amount saved first. A ceiling on what the family borrows. A rule on which requests get a yes and which get a no.

Write the answers down and keep the sheet. Next quarter, compare.

## Make it safe to say no

Family is expected to help family, and that is not a flaw. But unplanned giving is a real drain: K1,000 here, K500 there, and by year's end the money is gone and nothing was decided.

Use a four-step answer, so that a no is a decision rather than a betrayal:

1. **Acknowledge** — "I hear you, this matters."
2. **Clarify** — "How much, for what, and by when?"
3. **Evaluate** — "Can I do this without touching the school fees?"
4. **Decide** — "Yes, I can send K500 this month." Or: "Not this month, but I can help you on payday."

**Never give money you do not have, and never borrow to give.** Budget a fixed family-help amount each month and let the budget decide.

## Three habits to show children

Children copy what they see, so show them the sequence rather than lecturing them.

| Habit | How a child sees it |
|---|---|
| **Save a fixed amount first** | On payday, money moves into the savings place before anything is spent. The amount is fixed, not decided by mood |
| **Keep it somewhere boring and safe** | A second wallet or a bank account, not the one you shop from. Inflation was **6.1%** in September 2026, so a savings account paying 2–4% is losing purchasing power every year |
| **Let it grow** | Leave it alone and let the interest work. A 6-month deposit paying **7.4%** beat inflation by about 1.3 points — but the point is the habit, not the rate |

For a goal with a date the arithmetic is simple: **goal amount divided by paydays left = the transfer on payday**, rounded up. If school fees are K12,000 and there are six paydays left, that is K2,000 a month, every month.

## The conversation nobody wants to have: what if the breadwinner dies

This is exactly what an insurance policy is for, and why the **Insurance & Risk Protection for Civil Servants** module in this hub is worth a member's time.

A **funeral policy** pays a cash sum to the nominated beneficiary when the insured person dies, so the family does not have to sell assets or borrow in the middle of a bereavement. Two things to tell your family now:

- **Waiting periods are real.** Funeral policies in Zambia carry waiting periods of 3–6 months. If the insured person dies inside that window, **nothing is paid**.
- **A claim is paperwork, not a favour.** The claim must usually be submitted within **6 months** of the death and the supporting documents within **12 months**.

A Zambian funeral is widely estimated at **K4,000–K20,000** — an industry estimate, not an official statistic. It is why funeral cover of K10,000–K50,000 is meaningful rather than decorative, and why "we will manage" is not a plan.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Hold one 30-minute money talk with your household and write down the four answers: earnings, debts, savings, rules.
> 2. Fix one amount to move to savings on every payday, and name the goal it is for.
> 3. Optional: ask an insurer for its Key Fact Statement (the Pensions and Insurance Authority now issues these) and the current premium for a funeral policy covering you.

> **Where to check**
> The Bank of Zambia — for the FinScope inclusion and financial health figures and the quarterly Interest Rates and Bank Charges publication.
